lines: That earlier guarantee covered one sender, one lane, one session — nothing wider.
Now picture a step that reads one thing and writes several things in response.
All of those writes need to land together, or none of them should land at all.
From here on, a sender can carry a fixed identity that survives being restarted.
A separate, dedicated role somewhere else keeps track of every one of these all-or-nothing steps.
It remembers exactly where each one stands, independent of the data itself.
Worth reasoning through before the reveal settles it.
A sender restarts under that same fixed identity, but its old copy is still writing somewhere.
What happens to whatever that old, forgotten copy is still trying to send?
answer: It gets turned away outright, every single time.
The restart hands out a fresh marker that outranks the old one completely.
Anything still arriving under that stale marker is recognized and rejected on the spot.

lines: The restart itself is what triggers a brand new, higher marker to take over.
Nothing under the old marker ever gets folded in or merged with the new one.
An old copy that hasn't noticed the restart yet simply loses, every time.
Worth reasoning through before this reveal settles it too.
One of these all-or-nothing steps gets called off partway through, but its writes are still sitting right there.
Does an ordinary reader coming along afterward see those called-off writes?
answer: That depends entirely on which reading mode got picked.
Nothing ever actually gets erased because of the call-off, not a single byte.
One mode shows everything regardless; the other quietly screens out whatever got called off.

lines: One reading mode just shows everything, called off or not, with no screening at all.
The stricter mode only hands back writes from steps that actually went through to completion.
It does that screening up to a tracked boundary, not by deleting anything upstream.
Here's where this closes a gap named much earlier in this chapter.
Marking what was read and writing what comes out of it now happen as one single step.
Either both of those land together, or neither one does, no exceptions.
One newer safeguard stops a step that gets stuck half-finished from blocking every strict reader behind it forever.
A separate, newer addition lets something entirely outside this system join one of these all-or-nothing steps too.
Named here, not built here — no second real system is running in this sandbox to demonstrate it against.
Every figure shown so far came from one real run, happening just now, of this topic's own toy model.
The old copy getting turned away, right on cue.
And the called-off write showing up under one reading mode while staying hidden under the other.
So: a fixed identity survives a restart, and a separate role tracks every all-or-nothing step.
One reading mode screens out what got called off; the other shows everything regardless.
And marking what was read now rides inside that very same all-or-nothing step.
